questions.explanation: Sensitive information filters accept custom regex patterns, such as a booking ID format, and can mask matches in model responses. Denied topics and word filters do not match a pattern.
whyWrong: A denied topic blocks a subject of conversation. It does not find and mask a code pattern.
A word filter needs an exact list, and new codes are issued with every booking.
A grounding check detects answers not supported by the source. It does not mask codes.

questions.stem: A RAG assistant on Amazon Bedrock sometimes replies with accurate statements copied from the retrieved documents that do not answer what the customer asked. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails policy detects this?
options: Contextual grounding check
Sensitive information filter
Word filter
Prompt attack filter
questions.explanation: A contextual grounding check scores relevance as well as grounding. The relevance score flags a response that is grounded in the source but does not answer the user's query.
whyWrong: A sensitive information filter detects personal data, not answers that miss the question.
A word filter blocks listed words; it cannot judge whether an answer fits the question.
A prompt attack filter inspects user inputs for jailbreaks, not responses.

questions.stem: Visitors to a parts catalog type an exact part number and need the matching product page. A developer proposes adding a large language model to find it. Which choice best supports the company's sustainability goals?
options: Fine-tune a model to memorize part numbers
Use a standard database lookup
Use the largest available model
Run an always-on GPU endpoint
questions.explanation: AWS sustainability guidance says to ask first whether generative AI is the right tool. A simple lookup achieves the same outcome with far fewer resources.
whyWrong: Fine-tuning uses heavy compute for something an exact lookup already does.
The largest model uses the most energy, for a task that needs no generation.
An always-on GPU endpoint wastes energy while idle.

questions.stem: A company is reviewing legal and business risks before launching a public generative AI feature built on Amazon Bedrock. Which two risks should it include? (Choose two.)
options: Biased outputs causing discrimination complaints
Harmful outputs damaging customer trust
Amazon Bedrock training base models on its prompts
Model providers reading its prompts in Amazon Bedrock
AWS taking legal responsibility for generated content
questions.explanation: Biased outputs can bring legal exposure, and harmful outputs can erode customer trust. Both appear among the recognized legal and business risks of generative AI. Amazon Bedrock does not use prompts to train base models or share them with model providers, and the company stays responsible for the content it generates.
whyWrong: Amazon Bedrock does not use customer prompts or outputs to train base models.
Model providers have no access to customer prompts and completions in Amazon Bedrock.
The customer, not AWS, is responsible for content generated with Amazon Bedrock.

questions.stem: A marketing agency will generate ad copy and images with a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Its legal team's top concern is third-party claims that the generated outputs infringe copyrights. Which choice most directly reduces the agency's exposure to this risk?
options: Use a generally available Amazon Nova model
Turn on Bedrock model invocation logging
Add a guardrail word filter
Raise the temperature setting
questions.explanation: AWS offers uncapped intellectual property indemnity for outputs of generally available Amazon Nova models, protecting customers from third-party claims that those outputs infringe IP, including copyright.
whyWrong: Logging stores outputs for review but does not reduce legal liability.
A word filter blocks listed words; it does not protect against copyright claims.
Temperature changes randomness; it does not reduce legal liability.

questions.stem: A team labels photos with the emotion shown. All its annotators live in one region, and the trained model misreads expressions common elsewhere. What should the team do to improve the dataset?
options: Remove the misread examples
Add annotators from varied regions
Train longer on the same labels
Switch to a larger model
questions.explanation: Diverse annotators reduce blind spots in labels, making the dataset more representative.
whyWrong: Removing hard examples hides the gap instead of fixing the labels.
Longer training on biased labels keeps the bias.
A bigger model learns the same biased labels.

questions.stem: A data scientist wants a more reliable estimate of how well a model generalizes by repeatedly training on part of the data and validating on the held-out part. Which technique does this?
options: K-fold cross-validation
Early stopping of the training run
L1 regularization of the model weights
Bagging with several parallel models
questions.explanation: K-fold cross-validation uses each data subset once as validation data and averages the scores, revealing overfitting.
whyWrong: Early stopping is a prevention method, not an estimate by repeated splits.
Regularization penalizes complexity during training; it estimates nothing.
Bagging combines models to reduce variance; it is not a validation scheme.

questions.stem: A lender tests its approval model by changing only an applicant's gender in otherwise identical records and checking whether the decision changes. Which approach is this?
options: K-fold cross-validation across several data splits
Random oversampling of the minority class in the training data
Counterfactual fairness testing of paired records
Hyperparameter tuning of the learning rate and batch size
questions.explanation: Swapping a sensitive characteristic and seeing whether the decision changes is counterfactual fairness testing.
whyWrong: Cross-validation estimates generalization, not group treatment.
Oversampling changes class balance; it does not test decisions.
Tuning hyperparameters improves training and does not test for bias.

questions.stem: A regulator asks why a complex model denied one specific applicant. Which output best answers the question?
options: The model's overall accuracy and error rate on a held-out test set
Feature attributions showing each input's effect on that decision
The training loss curve from the most recent training run
A list of the hyperparameters used during training
questions.explanation: Per-prediction feature attributions, such as Shapley values, explain the contribution of each input to an individual decision.
whyWrong: Overall accuracy describes the whole model, not one decision.
A loss curve shows training progress, not why a decision was made.
Hyperparameters describe configuration, not an individual outcome.

questions.stem: A lender's responsible AI team separates its transparency work from its explainability work. Which deliverable is mainly a transparency measure rather than an explanation of model outputs?
options: Feature attributions for one applicant's score
Published notes on intended uses and limits
A partial dependence plot for income
A counterfactual for one rejected decision
questions.explanation: Explainability is about understanding and evaluating system outputs, and transparency is about enabling stakeholders to make informed choices about engaging with the system. Documenting intended uses and limitations informs those choices; attributions, partial dependence and counterfactuals explain outputs.
whyWrong: Feature attributions explain one output.
A partial dependence plot explains how outputs respond to a feature.
A counterfactual explains what would change one output.

questions.stem: Before choosing a model for a public question-answering tool, a governance team wants documented, comparable evidence for each candidate model on Amazon Bedrock: how often it produces harmful language and how often its answers are correct. The team has no prompt dataset of its own. Which two metrics should it select in an automatic model evaluation job with built-in datasets? (Choose two.)
options: Robustness, which measures how much answers change when prompts contain small typos
Toxicity, which scores generated responses for harmful content
Grounding, which checks responses against retrieved source passages
Accuracy, which compares responses with reference answers in the dataset
Latency, which measures how long each candidate model takes to respond
questions.explanation: Automatic model evaluation in Amazon Bedrock reports accuracy, robustness, and toxicity, with built-in datasets for each. Toxicity covers harmful content and accuracy covers correctness; robustness measures how output shifts under small perturbations such as typos.
whyWrong: Robustness measures sensitivity to minor input changes, not harm or correctness.
Grounding checks are a Guardrails runtime feature, not an automatic evaluation metric.
Latency is not one of the automatic evaluation metrics and says nothing about harm or correctness.

questions.stem: A bank's assistant on Amazon Bedrock uses a guardrail. Product owners want customers told clearly when a request cannot be answered. The security team warns that revealing which filter fired, and at what strength, would help attackers probe the guardrail. Which approach balances both concerns?
options: Return the full guardrail trace to customers
Turn off the guardrail for customer chats
Echo the prompt with the matched filter highlighted
Show a custom blocked message without filter details
questions.explanation: A guardrail includes messaging for blocked prompts and responses, and the team can replace the default text with its own. A clear, generic decline keeps users informed while withholding the filter details attackers could use.
whyWrong: The trace shows which filter fired, exactly what the security team wants hidden.
Turning the guardrail off removes the protection altogether.
Highlighting the matched filter shows attackers what triggered the block.

questions.stem: An Amazon Bedrock agent uses an action group backed by an AWS Lambda function that issues refunds. Security wants only that one agent to be able to invoke the function. Which configuration applies least privilege?
options: A function policy that allows only that agent
A function policy that allows any Bedrock agent
A guardrail that denies refund topics
A KMS key that encrypts the function
questions.explanation: Bedrock invokes an action group's Lambda function through a resource-based policy on the function. Scoping that policy to the specific agent's ARN limits invocation to that one agent, which is least privilege.
whyWrong: Allowing any agent is broader than needed. Other agents could issue refunds.
A guardrail filters conversation content. It does not control which agents can call the function.
Encryption protects data. It does not control who can invoke the function.

questions.stem: A company requires that every model inference call its developers make through Amazon Bedrock includes the approved guardrail. Requests without it must fail, whichever application sends them. Which approach enforces this?
options: Weekly reviews of invocation logs
An IAM policy that requires the guardrail
A system prompt that requests the guardrail
A KMS key that encrypts the guardrail
questions.explanation: An IAM policy can deny any inference request that does not include the specified guardrail. Enforcement then happens when the request is authorized, whichever application sends it.
whyWrong: Log reviews find missing guardrails after the fact. They do not make the requests fail.
A prompt cannot make a request fail. Applying the guardrail happens outside the model.
Encrypting the guardrail protects its configuration. It does not make inference require it.

questions.stem: A data lake table used to train a churn model holds customer behavior fields plus social security numbers and birth dates. Data scientists must query the table for training but must never see those two fields. Which solution meets this requirement?
options: Amazon Macie
AWS Key Management Service
AWS Lake Formation
AWS Glue DataBrew
questions.explanation: Lake Formation data filters provide column-level security, so the data scientists can query the table while the excluded personal fields never appear in their results.
whyWrong: Macie discovers sensitive data; it does not control who can see columns.
KMS encrypts data at rest; anyone allowed to read the table still sees every column.
DataBrew profiles and prepares data; it does not control column access.

questions.stem: A regulated lender must prove that the dataset used to train a credit model was not altered or deleted for five years after training. No one, including administrators, may be able to change it during that time. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Amazon S3 Object Lock
Amazon S3 Versioning
Amazon S3 Lifecycle rules
AWS CloudTrail data events
questions.explanation: Object Lock stores objects as write-once-read-many. In compliance mode no user, including the root user, can overwrite or delete a locked version or shorten its retention.
whyWrong: Versioning keeps old versions, but administrators can still delete them.
Lifecycle rules move or delete data; they do not prevent changes.
CloudTrail records changes after they happen; it does not prevent them.

questions.stem: A company's Amazon Bedrock guardrail blocks prompts that contain customer card numbers, and model invocation logging is turned on. An audit later finds card numbers from the blocked prompts stored in plain text. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Model invocation logging stored the blocked prompts
The guardrail checked only model responses
AWS KMS key rotation exposed old log entries
Amazon Macie copied the numbers during a scan
questions.explanation: Content blocked by guardrail policies still appears as plain text in model invocation logs when logging is enabled. Turning off invocation logging, or keeping that content out of the logs, closes the leak.
whyWrong: The guardrail did block the prompts, so it was checking input.
Key rotation does not decrypt or expose old data.
Macie reports where sensitive data is; it does not copy it into logs.

questions.stem: An HR assistant uses RAG over the company's policy documents. When the retrieved passages do not cover a question, it still gives a confident, invented policy. Which change best grounds its answers?
options: Fine-tune the model on policies quarterly
Instruct it to answer only from retrieved passages
Block policy questions with a denied topic
Add examples of confident policy answers
questions.explanation: Grounding instructions limit the model to the retrieved content and tell it to say it does not know when the answer is missing, so it stops filling gaps with invented policy.
whyWrong: Quarterly fine-tuning does not stop it inventing answers between updates.
Blocking the topic stops the assistant answering policy questions at all.
Confident examples make invented answers sound surer.

questions.stem: A healthcare company subject to HIPAA must have a Business Associate Addendum with AWS before it processes protected health information in its AI workloads. Where can it review and accept this agreement?
options: AWS Config
AWS Artifact
AWS Trusted Advisor
Amazon Inspector
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact lets customers review, accept, and track agreements with AWS, such as a BAA, in addition to downloading compliance reports.
whyWrong: Config records resource configuration and compliance, not agreements.
Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations, not legal agreements.
Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, not agreements.

questions.stem: An auditor asks for a record of which IAM principals downloaded individual files from the Amazon S3 bucket that holds a model's training data. Which AWS service records this activity?
options: AWS CloudTrail
AWS Config
Amazon Inspector
Amazon Macie
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records API activity, including who made each call. Object-level reads such as GetObject are data events, which a trail logs once data events are turned on for the bucket.
whyWrong: Config tracks resource configuration changes, not who read each object.
Inspector scans workloads for vulnerabilities; it does not log object reads.
Macie finds sensitive data in Amazon S3; it does not record who downloaded each file.

questions.stem: A company runs AI workloads in several accounts. Its governance team wants to check continuously that resources, such as S3 buckets holding training data, stay encrypted and logged, and to flag any that drift out of compliance. Which service should it use?
options: AWS CloudTrail
AWS Artifact
Amazon Inspector
AWS Config
questions.explanation: AWS Config evaluates resource configurations against rules and flags noncompliant resources, continuously as they change. Conformance packs bundle rules and remediation to deploy them as one unit across accounts.
whyWrong: CloudTrail records API activity. It does not judge whether resource settings comply.
Artifact provides AWS's own compliance reports, not checks on the company's resources.
Inspector scans for software vulnerabilities, not configuration settings such as encryption.

questions.stem: A company's data governance policy for an Amazon Bedrock application has two rules. Overwritten or deleted training files in Amazon S3 must stay recoverable, and model invocation logs sent to Amazon CloudWatch Logs must be deleted automatically after one year. Which two actions meet these rules? (Choose two.)
options: Move the training files to S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Disable invocation logging after one year
Enable S3 Versioning on the training bucket
Turn on CloudTrail data events for the bucket
Set the log group retention to one year
questions.explanation: S3 Versioning keeps every version of an object, so overwritten or deleted files can be restored. CloudWatch Logs keeps log data indefinitely by default, and a log group retention setting deletes events older than the chosen period.
whyWrong: Archiving lowers cost but does not keep overwritten or deleted versions.
Disabling logging stops new logs but does not delete old ones.
CloudTrail records who changed files; it cannot restore them.

questions.stem: A company's AI policy sets minimum quality levels and a regular evaluation schedule for its generative AI assistant. The team then fine-tunes the model, and a manager suggests skipping the next scheduled evaluation because the base model already passed. What does good governance require?
options: Skip evaluation until users report problems
Apply the same criteria and schedule
Evaluate only the base model
Review it once at launch instead
questions.explanation: Customized and fine-tuned models should meet the same evaluation criteria and cadence as non-customized models, in line with the organization's AI policy.
whyWrong: Waiting for user reports lets problems reach users, and fine-tuning can change behavior.
Fine-tuning changes the model, so the base model's results do not carry over.
A one-time review drops the regular schedule the policy requires.

questions.stem: A company is setting up governance for its generative AI workloads. Which two actions support its governance process? (Choose two.)
options: Assign a named owner to each workload
Run periodic evaluations against ground truth
Let each team set its own standards
Evaluate the model only at launch
Keep evaluation results within the team
questions.explanation: Governance defines policy, owners, and minimum performance levels, then checks them on a regular cadence against ground truth data that is refreshed as usage changes.
whyWrong: Governance needs a common policy, including minimum performance levels.
Model performance can drift as usage changes, so checks must continue after launch.
Hiding results undermines the oversight that governance depends on.

questions.stem: A security team logs millions of staff sign-ins with time, place, and device. Confirmed attacks are rare and were never labeled. The team wants a model that learns normal sign-in behavior from the unlabeled data and flags sign-ins that don't fit. Which approach fits?
options: A binary classification model
An autoencoder neural network
A linear regression model
A reinforcement learning agent
questions.explanation: An autoencoder trains on unlabeled data and learns to rebuild normal inputs from a compressed form. Sign-ins it rebuilds poorly have a large reconstruction error, so they stand out as anomalies.
whyWrong: A binary classifier needs labeled examples of attacks, and none exist.
Linear regression predicts a number from labeled examples. It does not learn what normal looks like.
Reinforcement learning learns actions from rewards, not patterns in logged data.

questions.stem: A payments team wants to give every incoming transaction a score for how unusual it is. The team has no labels that mark fraud. Which Amazon SageMaker AI built-in algorithm fits?
options: XGBoost
Linear Learner
Random Cut Forest
Factorization Machines
questions.explanation: Random Cut Forest is the SageMaker AI built-in algorithm for anomaly detection. It is unsupervised, so it needs no fraud labels, and it gives each data point an anomaly score.
whyWrong: XGBoost is a supervised algorithm. It learns from examples labeled fraud or not fraud, and the team has none.
Linear Learner is a supervised algorithm for classification or regression. It needs labeled examples.
Factorization Machines is a supervised algorithm for classification or regression on sparse data. It needs labeled examples.

questions.stem: A grocery chain wants to find natural groupings among its 400 stores based on sales mix, foot traffic, and basket size, so it can plan store formats. Nobody has defined the groups in advance. Which type of ML task is this?
options: Anomaly detection
Dimensionality reduction (PCA)
Clustering
Time-series forecasting
questions.explanation: Clustering is unsupervised: it finds groups in unlabeled data on its own. No predefined group labels exist here, so the algorithm must discover them.
whyWrong: Anomaly detection finds the few stores that are unusual; it does not sort all stores into groups.
PCA shrinks many measures into fewer ones; it does not assign stores to groups.
Forecasting predicts future values over time, such as next month's sales; it does not group stores.

questions.stem: A team's neural network scores 99% accuracy on its training data but 71% on validation data. The team cannot collect more data this quarter. Which two changes most directly address the problem? (Choose two.)
options: Add dropout layers
Train for more epochs
Increase L2 regularization
Increase the learning rate
Add more layers and parameters
questions.explanation: The gap between training and validation accuracy is overfitting. Dropout and L2 regularization discourage memorizing the training data, and neither needs new data.
whyWrong: More epochs on the same data lets the model memorize it even more.
A higher learning rate changes training speed and stability; it does not stop memorization.
A bigger network can memorize more, which worsens overfitting.

questions.stem: An ML team must keep a record of every trained model version, with its metrics and whether a reviewer approved it for production, before anything is deployed. Which SageMaker AI capability fits?
options: SageMaker Model Registry
SageMaker Feature Store
SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker Data Wrangler
questions.explanation: Model Registry catalogs model versions with their metadata and an approval status, so only approved versions move to deployment.
whyWrong: Feature Store keeps reusable features for training and inference, not model versions.
Ground Truth labels data; it does not track models.
Data Wrangler prepares data; it does not record model approvals.

questions.stem: A legal search tool keeps returning passages about riverbanks when lawyers search for bank mergers. Its embedding model gives a word the same vector in every sentence. The team wants each word's vector to reflect the sentence around it. What should it use?
options: A static word-embedding model
A contextual embedding model
A larger keyword index
A lower temperature setting
questions.explanation: A static model such as Word2Vec gives "bank" one vector everywhere. A contextual model such as BERT reads the surrounding words, so "bank" in a merger sentence gets a different embedding from "bank" by a river.
whyWrong: A static model gives each word one vector, which is the cause of the problem.
A keyword index matches words, so it still cannot tell the two meanings of bank apart.
Temperature affects how a model writes text, not how search matches meanings.

questions.stem: At a retailer, SQL analysts, data engineers, and ML developers each sign in to different consoles. An administrator wants them to sign in once, work on shared projects with access-controlled data, and include Amazon Bedrock capabilities. Which AWS offering fits?
options: AWS Glue Studio
SageMaker Unified Studio
Amazon Q Developer
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
questions.explanation: SageMaker Unified Studio brings AWS data, analytics, ML, and generative AI tools into one environment, where administrators give people access and teams work in governed projects.
whyWrong: Glue Studio builds data integration jobs; it is one data tool, not a shared environment for all three roles.
Q Developer helps individual developers write code; it is not a shared data and AI workspace.
Canvas lets business analysts build ML models without code; it does not bring all three roles into shared projects.

questions.stem: A training lead wants staff to practice prompting by building small generative AI apps from plain-language descriptions, with no code to write and no AWS account to set up. Which option fits?
options: Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio
PartyRock
questions.explanation: PartyRock is an Amazon Bedrock playground for building and sharing no-code generative AI mini-apps, made for learning and experimenting.
whyWrong: Canvas builds ML models without code, but inside an AWS account; it is not a prompt playground.
AgentCore runs production agents and needs engineering work.
Unified Studio is a governed team environment in an AWS account, more than a practice tool needs.

questions.stem: A team wants to fine-tune an open-weight model and host it on instance types it selects and manages itself. Which service fits best?
options: Amazon SageMaker JumpStart
Amazon Bedrock model customization
Amazon Q Business
Amazon Comprehend
questions.explanation: JumpStart offers pretrained models that you can fine-tune and deploy on SageMaker AI instances you choose and control.
whyWrong: Bedrock runs customization as a managed service; you do not choose or manage the instances.
Q Business is a ready-made assistant over company data, not a model hub.
Comprehend is a pretrained text analysis service; you do not fine-tune open models with it.

questions.stem: A travel company wants to turn each hotel's amenity list into a short, friendly paragraph for its website. Which AWS service fits?
options: Amazon Textract
Amazon Bedrock
Amazon Translate
Amazon Kendra
questions.explanation: Writing new text from a few facts is a generative task, which Amazon Bedrock's foundation models do.
whyWrong: Textract reads text out of documents; it does not write new text.
Translate changes text from one language to another; it does not compose paragraphs.
Kendra finds answers in existing documents; it does not write new copy.

questions.stem: A mining company has thousands of internal geology reports but no question-and-answer pairs. Using SageMaker JumpStart, it wants to change the model's weights so the model learns the company's specialist vocabulary. Which approach fits?
options: Instruction-based fine-tuning
Domain adaptation fine-tuning
Reinforcement learning from human feedback
Retrieval Augmented Generation
questions.explanation: Domain adaptation fine-tuning trains a model on plain domain text, such as reports, so it works with industry jargon and technical terms. It changes the model's weights and needs no question-and-answer pairs.
whyWrong: Instruction-based fine-tuning needs prompt and response pairs, and the company has none.
RLHF trains from human ratings of model answers. The company has reports, not ratings.
RAG retrieves documents at query time and leaves the weights unchanged. The company wants the model itself to learn.

questions.stem: An equipment maker has 40,000 unlabeled engineering manuals and no labeled examples. It wants a model in Amazon Bedrock to absorb the manuals' domain knowledge. Which customization method fits this data?
options: Continued pre-training
Supervised fine-tuning
Reinforcement fine-tuning
Model distillation
questions.explanation: Continued pre-training learns domain knowledge from unlabeled text, so it suits a large set of manuals. Supervised fine-tuning would need labeled input and output examples.
whyWrong: Supervised fine-tuning needs labeled prompt and answer pairs, which the company does not have.
Reinforcement fine-tuning learns from reward feedback on responses, not from raw manuals.
Distillation transfers a larger model's behavior to a smaller one; it does not add knowledge from the manuals.

questions.stem: A developer wants the model to pick each next token from exactly the 20 most likely candidates, however the probability is spread among them. Which inference parameter should the developer set?
options: Top P
Temperature
Top K
Response length
questions.explanation: Top K sets the number of most-likely candidates the model considers for the next token, so the pool is a fixed size.
whyWrong: Top P keeps a percentage of the probability, so the number of candidates changes from token to token.
Temperature reshapes the probabilities; it does not set how many candidates are considered.
Response length limits how long the response is, not which tokens are considered.

questions.stem: A team wants the set of candidate tokens to shrink when the model is confident and grow when it is unsure, keeping only the likeliest tokens that together make up 90% of the probability. Which parameter does this?
options: Temperature
Top P
Top K
Repetition penalty
questions.explanation: Top P sets the percentage of most-likely candidates the model considers: the top P% of the cumulative probability. The number of tokens in that share changes with how the probability is spread.
whyWrong: Temperature reshapes the probabilities but does not cut the pool to a share.
Top K always considers the same number of candidates.
A repetition penalty discourages repeated tokens; it does not set the candidate pool.

questions.stem: An accounts team wants a model to pull the payment due date out of supplier emails and always return it as YYYY-MM-DD. They will put a few examples in the prompt. What should each example contain?
options: The YYYY-MM-DD format on its own, with no sample emails
A sample supplier email paired with its due date as YYYY-MM-DD
A sample supplier email paired with a polite reply to it
A sample due date paired with the supplier's company name
questions.explanation: Few-shot examples show the mapping the model should copy: an input like the ones it will see, paired with exactly the output it should give.
whyWrong: A format alone is zero-shot; it shows no email-to-date examples.
A reply shows how to answer the email, not how to extract the date.
A date and a name leave out the email the model has to read.

questions.stem: A skin-condition model is less accurate for patients with darker skin tones, who make up a small share of its training images. Which step most directly addresses the cause?
options: Longer training on the existing set of images
A larger model architecture
Data augmentation for underrepresented groups
Stronger L2 regularization
questions.explanation: The cause is imbalanced data. Data augmentation creates new examples for the groups with few images, which helps balance the dataset.
whyWrong: More training on the same imbalanced images keeps the same gap.
A bigger model still learns from too few examples of darker skin tones.
Regularization reduces overfitting in general; it does not add examples for the missing groups.

questions.stem: A lender must tell one rejected applicant which factors drove that specific decision. Which explanation method fits?
options: SHAP feature attributions
A partial dependence plot
A confusion matrix
A model card
questions.explanation: Shapley values assign each feature an importance for one particular prediction, so they explain a single applicant's outcome. A partial dependence plot instead shows a feature's effect across the whole dataset.
whyWrong: A partial dependence plot shows a feature's average effect across all applicants, not one decision.
A confusion matrix summarizes overall prediction errors, not the reasons for one decision.
A model card documents the model's purpose and limits, not why one applicant was rejected.

questions.stem: A bank's savings assistant must not discuss cryptocurrency investing, even when customers ask politely and use no harmful language. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails feature fits?
options: Content filters
Denied topics
Automated Reasoning checks
Sensitive information filters
questions.explanation: Denied topics block a subject you describe in plain language, by meaning, whatever words are used. Content filters cover predefined harm categories, and a polite investing question is not harmful.
whyWrong: Content filters catch harmful categories such as hate or violence; a polite investing question falls in none.
Automated Reasoning checks test answers against logic rules you define; they do not block a subject.
Sensitive information filters find PII, not subjects.

questions.stem: A company will fine-tune a model on HR chat transcripts, which include employee names and staff IDs, so it can draft answers to policy questions. The model must not be able to learn or repeat any real employee's details. Which two steps meet this goal? (Choose two.)
options: Require MFA to open the transcript bucket
Replace names and staff IDs with surrogate tokens
Lower the fine-tuned model's temperature
Train on synthetic transcripts with realistic patterns
Encrypt the transcripts with a KMS key
questions.explanation: Both right answers keep real people out of the training data. Masking swaps real identifiers for realistic but false values. Synthetic data replaces personal records with generated ones that keep the same patterns. With no real details in training, the model cannot memorize or repeat them.
whyWrong: MFA controls who opens the bucket. The real names still go into training.
Temperature changes how varied the output is. It does not remove names the model has learned.
Encryption protects the files at rest. The real names are still used for training.

questions.stem: An internal help assistant answers from a Bedrock knowledge base and sometimes quotes vendor contract numbers found in the documents it retrieves. The numbers follow a fixed pattern, and the documents must stay in the knowledge base. The numbers must be masked in every response, even if the model ignores its instructions. What should the team use?
options: A Guardrails regex sensitive information filter
A lower temperature setting
A system prompt instruction to omit them
AWS CloudTrail logging
questions.explanation: A sensitive information filter can use a custom regex to find a pattern in responses and mask it, while the documents stay as they are. It enforces the rule outside the model.
whyWrong: Temperature changes randomness, not whether the numbers appear.
A model can ignore a prompt instruction, so it does not guarantee masking.
CloudTrail records API activity; it does not change responses.

questions.stem: A team runs SageMaker AI Random Cut Forest (RCF) over hourly website traffic to catch sudden spikes. What does RCF give back for each data point?
options: An anomaly score, where higher means more unusual
A fraud or not-fraud label learned from labeled examples
The number of the cluster each point was assigned to
A forecast of the next hour's traffic for the website
questions.explanation: RCF associates each data point with an anomaly score: low means normal, high means anomalous. Where to draw the line between them is up to the team.
whyWrong: RCF is unsupervised; it does not learn labels from examples.
Cluster numbers come from clustering algorithms such as k-means.
Predicting the next value is forecasting, not anomaly scoring.

questions.stem: While training, a team watches validation loss fall until epoch 12 and then rise, while training loss keeps falling. Which technique acts on exactly this signal?
options: Dropout, which switches off random neurons during training
Early stopping, which ends training when validation stops improving
Data augmentation, which creates new examples from existing data
Incremental training, which continues from an existing model
questions.explanation: Validation loss rising while training loss falls is the point where the model starts learning noise. Early stopping ends training there.
whyWrong: Dropout also reduces overfitting, but it changes training throughout rather than reacting to the validation curve.
Augmentation adds varied examples; it does not watch the validation curve.
Incremental training is for updating a model with new data, not for deciding when to stop.

questions.stem: Which of these produces a different vector for "charge" in "charge the battery" than in "a late-payment charge"?
options: BERT
Word2Vec
GloVe
Principal component analysis (PCA)
questions.explanation: BERT reads the words around each word, so the same word gets different embeddings in different sentences. Word2Vec and GloVe give each word one vector everywhere.
whyWrong: Word2Vec gives "charge" one vector in every sentence, so the two meanings stay mixed.
GloVe also gives each word a single fixed vector.
PCA reduces dimensions; it does not read context.

questions.stem: Which statement about PartyRock is correct?
options: It is an Amazon Bedrock playground for building no-code generative AI apps
It is a governed workspace where data and ML teams share projects
It is a SageMaker hub of models you deploy on instances you manage
It is an IDE where AI agents turn written specs into working code
questions.explanation: PartyRock is an Amazon Bedrock playground for building and sharing no-code generative AI apps, made for learning and experimenting.
whyWrong: That describes SageMaker Unified Studio.
That describes SageMaker JumpStart.
That describes Kiro.

questions.stem: For its next token, a model ranks four candidates with probabilities 0.6, 0.25, 0.1, and 0.05. Top P is set to 0.85. Which candidates can the model choose from?
options: Only the 0.6 candidate
The 0.6 and 0.25 candidates
The 0.6, 0.25 and 0.1 candidates
All four candidates
questions.explanation: Top P keeps the likeliest candidates until their probabilities add up to P. Here 0.6 + 0.25 = 0.85, so the two likeliest stay in the pool. AWS's own example works the same way: at Top P 0.9, candidates at 0.7 and 0.2 are both kept.
whyWrong: 0.6 alone falls short of 0.85, so the next candidate is also kept.
The pool is already complete at 0.85, so the 0.1 candidate is cut.
Top P cuts candidates from the pool. It does not just reweight all of them.

questions.stem: Continued pre-training in Amazon Bedrock learns from unlabeled text. What kind of data does fine-tuning learn from instead?
options: Labeled prompt-completion pairs
Unlabeled domain documents
Passages retrieved at answer time
Raw web text crawled at scale
questions.explanation: Fine-tuning teaches a task from labeled examples, each with a prompt and its ideal completion. Continued pre-training adds domain knowledge from unlabeled text.
whyWrong: Unlabeled domain text is what continued pre-training uses.
Retrieving passages at answer time is RAG, which does not train the model.
Large-scale raw web text is used to pre-train a foundation model, not to fine-tune it.

questions.stem: A team has 2,000 examples, each a customer request paired with the ideal written response, and wants the model itself to answer new requests in that way. Which customization fits?
options: A few of the examples in each prompt, with no training
Instruction tuning on the request-response pairs
Continued pre-training on unlabeled text
A higher Top K setting so answers vary more
questions.explanation: Instruction tuning is fine-tuning on instruction and response pairs, which is exactly what the team has, and it changes how the model itself responds.
whyWrong: Few-shot examples guide one prompt at a time; the model itself does not change.
Continued pre-training uses unlabeled text and would ignore the pairing.
Top K changes how varied the output is, not what the model has learned.

questions.stem: A retailer's shopping assistant must never write the names of two competitors. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails feature fits most directly?
options: Denied topics
Word filters
Content filters
Contextual grounding checks
questions.explanation: Word filters block exact words or phrases you list, such as competitor names. Denied topics block a whole subject by meaning, which is broader than two names.
whyWrong: Denied topics block a subject by meaning; two specific names are an exact-match job.
Content filters cover harm categories such as hate or violence; a competitor name is not one.
Grounding checks catch answers not supported by a source.

questions.stem: A game studio's chat assistant must block insulting or hateful replies, and the team wants to set how strictly each kind is filtered. Which Amazon Bedrock Guardrails feature fits?
options: Content filters
Word filters
Denied topics
Sensitive information filters
questions.explanation: Content filters detect predefined harm categories, including hate and insults, with a strength you set for each category.
whyWrong: Word filters need every offending word listed and have no strength setting.
Denied topics block subjects you define, not harm categories by strength.
Sensitive information filters find PII, not insults.

questions.stem: Which pairing of training problem and fix is right?
options: Few examples of one class: augment the data. Memorizing the training data: regularize
Few examples of one class: regularize. Memorizing the training data: augment the data
Few examples of one class: more epochs. Memorizing the training data: more layers
Few examples of one class: encrypt the data. Memorizing: lower the temperature
questions.explanation: Too few examples of a class is an imbalance, which data augmentation fixes by adding examples. Memorizing the training data is overfitting, which regularization curbs.
whyWrong: This swaps the two fixes.
More epochs and more layers both tend to make memorizing worse, and neither adds examples.
Encryption and temperature affect neither problem.

questions.stem: A bank wants to keep its real transaction records for training but replace account numbers with stand-in values that only a protected lookup table can turn back. What is this called?
options: Synthetic data generation
Data tokenization
Encryption at rest with AWS KMS
Model invocation logging
questions.explanation: Data tokenization swaps sensitive values for random stand-ins, with the link back kept in a secured token vault, so the records stay real but the identifiers are hidden.
whyWrong: Synthetic data replaces the records themselves with generated ones.
Encryption protects stored data, but training decrypts it and sees the real numbers.
Invocation logging records model requests; it does not hide identifiers.

questions.stem: A hospital wants developers to build and test a model on realistic patient records without any developer seeing a real patient's data. Which approach fits best?
options: Encrypt the real records with AWS KMS keys
Generate realistic artificial patient records
Lock the real records with S3 Object Lock
Give developers read-only access to real records
questions.explanation: Synthetic data keeps the statistical patterns of real data without containing real people, so developers work with realistic records and see no one's real data.
whyWrong: Developers who use the data still see it decrypted.
Object Lock stops changes or deletion; it does not hide the data.
Read-only access still shows real patients.
